questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had episodes of spinning for 2 weeks. They come on when he bends down to pick things off the floor and last about 10 seconds. Between episodes he feels well. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus or headache. Cranial nerve and cerebellar examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief (under 30 seconds) vertigo triggered by a change in head position with no hearing loss or neurological deficit is BPPV.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Seconds-long, positional, no hearing loss, normal neurology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPPV.

elim: Continuous vertigo for days with hearing loss.
Attacks last hours with hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
Vertigo with other brainstem features, not reproducible with posture.
Continuous vertigo for days after a viral illness, not seconds.

steps.x: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Seconds + head position + normal hearing and neurology = BPPV.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 3 weeks of brief vertigo when she turns over in bed. The left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces her vertigo with torsional nystagmus. Her ENT doctor arranges pure tone audiometry to help exclude other causes of vertigo.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on pure tone audiometry?
o: Normal hearing thresholds in both ears
questions.e: BPPV is a mechanical problem of canal debris, so hearing is normal.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on pure tone audiometry?
Positional vertigo with a positive Dix-Hallpike: BPPV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hearing is normal in BPPV.

elim: Presbycusis, unrelated to her vertigo.
Points to middle ear disease.
Typical of Ménière's disease.
Raises concern about vestibular schwannoma.

steps.x: D. Normal hearing thresholds in both ears. BPPV: no hearing loss, no neurological deficit.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had vertigo for 2 days. He describes it as spinning, worse when he moves his head. His GP is considering benign paroxysmal positional vertigo but wants to make sure a central cause is not being missed. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 162/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which additional feature would most suggest a central cause rather than BPPV?
o: Double vision and inability to walk unaided
Vertigo on rolling over in bed
questions.e: Vertigo with diplopia, ataxia, weakness, severe headache or another neurological deficit is a red flag for a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which additional feature would most suggest a central cause rather than BPPV?

clues: worse when he moves his head
steps.x: Positional worsening alone does not separate the two; neurological signs do.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diplopia and ataxia.

elim: Typical of BPPV.
Common in BPPV.
A recognised association of BPPV.
The classic BPPV trigger.

steps.x: A. Double vision and inability to walk unaided. Red flags in vertigo: neurological deficit, severe headache, ataxia, weakness or diplopia.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman lives alone and has osteoporosis. For 3 weeks she has had sudden brief spinning when she looks up to reach her kitchen cupboards or lies down in bed. The right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces her symptoms. She is waiting for treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most important complication of her condition?
questions.e: Sudden disabling vertigo makes falls the main complication, especially in a frail older woman with osteoporosis.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most important complication of her condition?

clues: looks up to reach her kitchen cupboards
steps.x: Sudden vertigo in a frail woman with fragile bones.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Falls (and fractures).

elim: BPPV does not affect the cochlea.
BPPV causes no neurological deficit.
BPPV is a peripheral disorder; it does not cause stroke.
Not a feature of BPPV.

steps.x: A. Falls. BPPV complication: falls.

questions.stem: A 52 year old painter has 10 days of sudden spinning that starts each time he tilts his head back to paint ceilings. Each attack lasts about 20 seconds and leaves him nauseated. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus, headache or weakness. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief vertigo triggered by neck extension, with no hearing loss or neurological deficit, is BPPV.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A positional trigger and seconds-long attacks.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPPV.

elim: Causes neck pain and stiffness, not brief spinning vertigo.
Hours-long attacks with hearing loss and tinnitus.
Brainstem symptoms, not isolated brief positional vertigo.
Usually with migraine headache, lasting minutes to hours.

steps.x: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Looking up, rolling, bending or neck extension triggering seconds of vertigo = BPPV.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has 1 week of brief spinning on lying down and rolling over in bed. Episodes last 15 seconds. He has hypertension treated with ramipril, type 2 diabetes, smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes a statin. He fell off a ladder and hit his head 2 weeks ago without loss of consciousness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor for his condition?
questions.e: BPPV is associated with recent head trauma and recent viral illness, which dislodge otoconia.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely predisposing factor for his condition?
Positional vertigo starting after a head injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Head trauma.

elim: Not a recognised cause of BPPV.
A vascular risk factor, not linked to BPPV.
Not linked to BPPV.
Not a recognised cause of BPPV.

steps.x: B. Recent head injury. BPPV associations: head trauma and recent viral illness.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has had dizzy spells for a month. She has been told she may have Ménière's disease or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. She has no headache. Her GP takes a careful history to tell them apart. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature of her history would most support benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
o: Episodes lasting under 30 seconds on turning her head
Fluctuating hearing loss in one ear
Sensation of fullness in one ear
questions.e: BPPV causes brief (<30 seconds) positional vertigo without hearing loss; Ménière's causes hours of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature of her history would most support benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?

clues: Ménière's disease or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
steps.x: Duration and hearing are the key discriminators.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Brief positional episodes.

elim: Typical of Ménière's disease.
Typical of Ménière's disease.
Typical of Ménière's disease.
Aural fullness is typical of Ménière's disease.

steps.x: B. Episodes lasting under 30 seconds on turning her head. BPPV: seconds, positional, normal hearing. Ménière's: hours, hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man takes amlodipine. For 2 weeks he has had brief spinning when he rolls over in bed or looks up at a high shelf. It does not happen when he stands up from a chair. Lying BP is 138/84 mmHg and standing BP after 3 minutes is 134/82 mmHg. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Spinning triggered by rolling over or looking up, not by standing, with no postural drop, is BPPV.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: rolls over in bed or looks up
does not happen when he stands up
steps.x: Head position, not body posture, is the trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPPV.

elim: Regular pulse and symptoms only with head position.
Occurs on standing, with a postural BP drop; neither is present.
Prodrome with loss of consciousness, not spinning on rolling over.
Would come with other brainstem symptoms.

steps.x: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. BPPV is triggered by head position (rolling, looking up), not by standing up.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has brief positional vertigo. During the right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre her eye movements are observed closely. Her doctor needs to decide whether the nystagmus is typical of a peripheral cause before diagnosing benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
questions.q: Which feature of the nystagmus best supports a diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
o: Changes direction with direction of gaze
Persists for minutes while the head is still
Torsional, starting after a few seconds and fading within 30 seconds
questions.e: In BPPV the Dix-Hallpike reproduces vertigo with torsional nystagmus towards the affected ear after a brief latency, and it is short-lived.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature of the nystagmus best supports a diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
Peripheral nystagmus has latency, is torsional and fatigues.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Torsional with latency, lasting under 30 seconds.

elim: Direction-changing nystagmus suggests a central cause.
Lack of latency suggests a central cause.
Persistent nystagmus suggests a central cause.
Downbeat nystagmus suggests a cerebellar or brainstem lesion.

steps.x: E. Torsional, starting after a few seconds and fading within 30 seconds. Positive Dix-Hallpike: latency, torsional nystagmus towards the affected ear, brief.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with atrial fibrillation has 2 weeks of brief spinning when he lies back in bed or turns his head quickly. Each lasts 10 seconds. He walks normally, speaks normally and has no double vision or headache. Cranial nerve, cerebellar and limb examination is normal. His pulse rate is 78 bpm, irregularly irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Despite AF, brief positional vertigo with completely normal neurological examination and no red flags is BPPV.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
No red flags and a typical positional history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPPV.

elim: AF is a risk factor, but stroke gives continuous vertigo with ataxia and neurological signs.
Continuous vertigo with hearing loss.
Hours-long attacks with hearing loss.
Progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus, not brief positional vertigo.

steps.x: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. AF does not make it a stroke: look for red flags; without them, brief positional vertigo is BPPV.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman had a flu-like illness 3 weeks ago. Her symptoms are shown on the timeline. Hearing is normal and she has no neurological symptoms. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.

visual.title: Her symptoms

events.x: Spinning for 15 seconds on rolling over in bed
Same brief spinning on looking up and bending down

visual.caption: Seconds-long attacks, each triggered by head position.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief positional vertigo after a viral illness, with normal hearing and no neurological deficit, is BPPV.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A viral illness, then seconds-long positional attacks.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPPV.

elim: Continuous vertigo with hearing loss during the illness.
Hours-long attacks with hearing loss and tinnitus.
Constant non-spinning unsteadiness lasting months.
Days of continuous vertigo during or soon after the illness, not brief positional attacks weeks later.

steps.x: B. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Recent viral illness is a recognised association of BPPV.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has brief vertigo when she lies down on her left side. The left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces her vertigo with torsional nystagmus after a short latency. She asks which part of her inner ear is causing the problem.
questions.q: Which structure is most likely to contain the displaced debris?
questions.e: Otoconia migrate from the utricle into a semicircular canal, usually the posterior one, which is the most dependent; the positive side is the affected ear.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which structure is most likely to contain the displaced debris?

clues: lies down on her left side
steps.x: A positive left test points to the left ear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The left posterior canal.

elim: Rarely affected; it lies uppermost and debris falls out of it.
The hearing organ; BPPV causes no hearing loss.
Involved in Ménière's disease.
Wrong side; the left test is positive and the horizontal canal is less common.

steps.x: D. Left posterior semicircular canal. BPPV: usually the posterior canal on the side of the positive Dix-Hallpike.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has had 2 weeks of brief spinning on looking up and turning in bed. Each episode lasts under 20 seconds. Neurological examination and hearing are normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Her GP wants to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: BPPV is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproducing vertigo with torsional nystagmus.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: brief spinning on looking up and turning in bed
Neurological examination and hearing are normal
steps.x: Typical BPPV history, no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dix-Hallpike.

elim: Not needed for typical positional vertigo without red flags.
Used in continuous vertigo to look for vestibular neuritis.
For asymmetric hearing loss and suspected schwannoma.
Hearing is normal and it does not confirm BPPV.

steps.x: B. Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre. Gold standard for BPPV: the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has 3 weeks of 15 second episodes of vertigo when rolling in bed. The right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces his vertigo with torsional nystagmus after brief latency. Neurological examination is normal and he has no headache. He asks for a brain scan to be safe.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A positive Dix-Hallpike with a typical history and no red flags confirms BPPV clinically; imaging is reserved for central features.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
The diagnosis is already confirmed clinically.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No imaging.

elim: Imaging is for red flags; he has none.
For seizures, not vertigo.
Indicated for central features such as ataxia, diplopia or weakness.
Specialist testing not needed when the Dix-Hallpike is positive.

steps.x: D. No further investigation is needed. BPPV is a clinical diagnosis; image only if red flags.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has brief positional vertigo. The left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre produces no vertigo or nystagmus. The right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre produces vertigo with torsional nystagmus beating towards the right ear, starting after 3 seconds and stopping after 20 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of these results?
questions.e: The affected ear is the side whose Dix-Hallpike reproduces torsional nystagmus towards that ear after a latency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely interpretation of these results?

clues: left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre produces no vertigo
steps.x: Only the right test is positive, with peripheral features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right posterior canal BPPV.

elim: Only the right test is positive.
Latency, torsion and fatigue all point to a peripheral cause.
The left test is negative.
Gives continuous vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus, not a positive Dix-Hallpike.

steps.x: D. Right posterior canal BPPV. The positive Dix-Hallpike side is the side to treat.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor is about to perform a Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre on a 58 year old woman with suspected right-sided benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. She has no neck problems. He asks his registrar how the test is done.
questions.q: Which is the correct way to perform the test on the right side?
o: Head turned 45° to the left, then lie back quickly
Head turned 45° to the right, then lie back quickly with the head hanging below the couch
Head turned 90° to the left, then sit up quickly
Head upright, patient stands up quickly from lying
Patient rolls slowly onto the right side with the head flexed
questions.e: The Dix-Hallpike turns the head 45° to the tested side and brings the patient rapidly supine with the neck extended, aligning the posterior canal with gravity.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the correct way to perform the test on the right side?
The test side is the side the head is turned towards.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 45° to the right, then rapidly back with head extended.

elim: Wrong direction and wrong movement.
That tests postural BP, not the semicircular canal.
That tests the left ear.
Too slow and the wrong plane to provoke the posterior canal.

steps.x: B. Head turned 45° to the right, then lie back quickly with the head hanging below the couch. Dix-Hallpike: turn 45° to the side being tested, lie back fast, watch for torsional nystagmus.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman attends the emergency department with 2 weeks of brief vertigo when she lies down or bends forward. She feels nauseated but has no hearing loss, tinnitus or headache. Her symptoms are reproduced on the right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: First-line treatment of BPPV is the Epley particle repositioning manoeuvre.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: no hearing loss, tinnitus or headache
steps.x: Confirmed BPPV without red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Epley manoeuvre.

elim: Used for Ménière's disease; not effective in BPPV.
A home option, not the first-line treatment when the Epley can be done.
Only short-term relief of nausea; it does not treat the cause.
No red flags.

steps.x: E. Epley manoeuvre. Confirmed BPPV: Epley first; prochlorperazine only for short-term nausea.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has had an Epley manoeuvre for confirmed left posterior canal BPPV. He is still very nauseated from his attacks today and has vomited once. He has no other symptoms and neurological examination is normal. He asks for something to settle the nausea for the next few days.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
questions.e: Prochlorperazine can be used short-term for nausea in BPPV; the Epley treats the cause.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate medication?
He needs short-term symptom relief only.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Short course of prochlorperazine.

elim: Sedating, slows vestibular compensation and risks dependence.
Ablative treatment for severe Ménière's disease.
For Ménière's disease, not BPPV.
Used in sudden hearing loss and some vestibular neuritis, not BPPV.

steps.x: E. Prochlorperazine for a few days. BPPV nausea: short-term prochlorperazine.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with confirmed right posterior canal BPPV does not want an Epley manoeuvre in clinic because she felt very sick during the Dix-Hallpike test. She works from home and would like something she can do by herself. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Brandt-Daroff exercises are a home treatment for BPPV that the patient performs herself.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: would like something she can do by herself
does not want an Epley manoeuvre
steps.x: A self-administered, home-based treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Brandt-Daroff exercises.

elim: Not effective for BPPV.
No role in BPPV.
Only short-term relief of nausea.
A destructive operation, not appropriate.

steps.x: B. Brandt-Daroff exercises. BPPV at home: Brandt-Daroff exercises.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has right posterior canal BPPV. She has had three Epley manoeuvres over 2 months, each giving only a short improvement, and she now feels generally unsteady between attacks. MRI brain is normal and neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent or recurrent BPPV is managed with repeat repositioning manoeuvres or vestibular rehabilitation; repeated Epleys have already failed.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Repeated Epleys have failed and she has ongoing unsteadiness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Vestibular rehabilitation.

elim: Not effective for BPPV.
For refractory Ménière's disease.
Delays compensation and has extrapyramidal side effects.
She is still disabled by symptoms.

steps.x: E. Vestibular rehabilitation. Persistent or recurrent BPPV: repeat manoeuvres or vestibular rehabilitation.

questions.stem: An 85 year old man has fallen twice in a month, each time when he lay back in bed and then got straight up during a bout of spinning. The left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces brief vertigo with torsional nystagmus. Neurological examination is normal. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management to reduce his falls?
questions.e: Treating the BPPV with an Epley manoeuvre removes the cause of the vertigo and so the falls.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate management to reduce his falls?

clues: left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces brief vertigo
steps.x: Falls caused by BPPV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the cause with Epley.

elim: No red flags.
Not effective in BPPV.
Do not treat the cause of his falls.
Increases falls risk in older people and does not treat BPPV.

steps.x: C. Epley manoeuvre. BPPV causing falls: Epley manoeuvre treats the cause.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with posterior canal BPPV asks where the loose crystals in her inner ear came from. Her ENT surgeon explains that calcium carbonate crystals normally sit on a sensory membrane elsewhere in the inner ear and have become dislodged.
questions.q: Which structure did the crystals most likely come from?
questions.e: Otoconia dislodge from the utricular macula and migrate into a semicircular canal.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which structure did the crystals most likely come from?
Otoconia live on the otolith organs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The utricular macula.

elim: Supports the organ of Corti and contains no otoconia.
The structure the debris disturbs, not its source.
Involved in endolymph resorption.
Contains cochlear nerve cell bodies.

steps.x: D. Macula of the utricle. BPPV: otoconia from the utricle drift into a semicircular canal.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has BPPV. A medical student notes that the posterior semicircular canal is affected in most patients and asks why this canal rather than the anterior or horizontal canal collects the dislodged otoconia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: It contains perilymph rather than endolymph
It is the most dependent canal when upright and lying
It lies closest to the cochlea
questions.e: Free otoconia fall under gravity into the most dependent canal, the posterior canal.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation?
Debris settles by gravity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The posterior canal is the lowest.

elim: All canals have a cupula.
All membranous canals contain endolymph.
Size is not the reason.
Proximity to the cochlea is not why debris settles there.

steps.x: D. It is the most dependent canal when upright and lying. Posterior canal is most affected because it is dependent.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman has BPPV of the right posterior canal. During the right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre her vertigo begins about 3 seconds after she lies back and stops within 20 seconds even though she stays in position.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her vertigo?
o: Otoconia moving in endolymph and deflecting the cupula
questions.e: Free-floating otoconia move under gravity through the endolymph, generating abnormal fluid flow that deflects the cupula; the delay is the time they take to move.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her vertigo?
Latency and short duration fit particles moving then settling.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Otoconia move endolymph and stimulate the cupula.

elim: Would cause brainstem ischaemia, not brief torsional nystagmus.
The mechanism of Ménière's disease.
Vestibular neuritis, with continuous vertigo.
Central, with no latency and neurological signs.

steps.x: E. Otoconia moving in endolymph and deflecting the cupula. Otoconia in the canal move with gravity, push endolymph and deflect the cupula.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with left posterior canal BPPV has torsional nystagmus during the left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre. His head is completely still on the couch. A student asks why his eyes are moving when his head is not.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the nystagmus?
o: False canal signal of head rotation drives the vestibulo-ocular reflex
questions.e: Otoconia stimulate the canal as if the head were rotating; the mismatch with real head movement drives the vestibulo-ocular reflex and produces nystagmus.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the nystagmus?
The canal reports movement that is not happening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Signal mismatch drives the VOR.

elim: Central nystagmus has no latency and comes with other signs.
Gives persistent gaze-evoked nystagmus.
Would cause diplopia, not rhythmic beating.
Causes papilloedema and headache, not positional nystagmus.

steps.x: D. False canal signal of head rotation drives the vestibulo-ocular reflex. BPPV nystagmus: a false rotation signal, mismatched with real head movement.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with right posterior canal BPPV is worried that she may lose her hearing or have a stroke. Her hearing and full neurological examination are normal. She asks why her doctor is confident that neither will happen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: BPPV affects both the cochlea and the canals equally
BPPV is caused by a small brainstem infarct
BPPV is caused by vestibular nerve inflammation
BPPV results from raised endolymph pressure
The problem is mechanical debris confined to a semicircular canal
questions.e: BPPV is purely mechanical canal debris, so there is no hearing loss and no brainstem or cerebellar sign.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: lose her hearing or have a stroke
Her hearing and full neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Mechanical canal problem, nothing else involved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mechanical canal debris.

elim: The cochlea is not involved.
That would cause neurological signs.
That is vestibular neuritis.
That is Ménière's disease, which affects hearing.

steps.x: E. The problem is mechanical debris confined to a semicircular canal. BPPV: canal debris only, so normal hearing and neurology.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man had an Epley manoeuvre for right posterior canal BPPV last week. Today the right Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre no longer produces vertigo or nystagmus. He asks why the treatment has stopped his attacks.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: The cupula has been surgically fixed
The otoconia have been returned to the utricle
The posterior canal has been blocked
The vestibular nerve has been desensitised
questions.e: The Epley uses gravity in a sequence of head positions to guide otoconia out of the semicircular canal back into the utricle, where they no longer stimulate the cupula.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation?
The particles are no longer in the canal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Otoconia moved back into the utricle.

elim: The Epley is non-surgical.
The manoeuvre moves, not dissolves, them.
That is canal plugging surgery.
The Epley does not act on the nerve.

steps.x: C. The otoconia have been returned to the utricle. Epley: gravity guides otoconia out of the canal into the utricle.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman had an Epley manoeuvre for left posterior canal BPPV 1 week ago. She is a little better but still has brief spinning when she rolls onto her left side. The left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre still reproduces vertigo with torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop all head movement for a month
questions.e: Persistent BPPV after one Epley is treated by repeating the repositioning manoeuvre (or vestibular rehabilitation).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: still reproduces vertigo with torsional nystagmus
steps.x: The Dix-Hallpike is still positive: debris remains in the canal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Repeat the Epley.

elim: Not effective in BPPV.
Destroys the inner ear; far too drastic.
Avoidance delays recovery and does not clear the canal.
A destructive operation, not appropriate.

steps.x: C. Repeat the Epley manoeuvre. Persistent BPPV: repeat repositioning manoeuvres.
